name: Range Map
why: Establish the ranges where you can score without staying available for the return.

mindset.intent: Control the space before increasing output.
mindset.focus: Notice where each fighter can land without overreaching.
mindset.reset: Return to the last range where you could see and react clearly.
mindset.anchor: Make them cross your range before they can attack.
mindset.context: Early-camp range study for a distance striker.

instructions: Mark the range where you can score while remaining difficult to reach.
Mark the range where the opponent becomes most dangerous.
Choose the strike that best controls the space between you.
Write one distance rule to test in your next technical session.
progress: Test the distance rule in technical work and keep it only if it holds up.

name: Lead-Hand Battle
why: Learn how the lead hand controls entry, rhythm and distance before exchanges develop.

mindset.intent: Own the first touch of the exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch what happens immediately after the jab or lead-hand feint.
mindset.reset: Rebuild the lead-hand position before throwing again.
mindset.anchor: Win the lead hand before chasing the rear hand.
mindset.context: Early-camp lead-hand control for a distance striker.

instructions: Identify the most common reaction to a jab or lead-hand feint.
Choose your lead-hand answer to that reaction.
Choose the follow-up that keeps you at your preferred range.
Write one lead-hand action you should avoid because it gives away distance.
progress: Use the chosen lead-hand answer during the next technical round.

name: Exit Discipline
why: Stop clean scoring from turning into avoidable return-fire by leaving on time.

mindset.intent: Finish the exchange with position, not admiration.
mindset.focus: Watch the half-second after your scoring action.
mindset.reset: If you stay too long, leave first and rebuild range.
mindset.anchor: Score, move, see again.
mindset.context: Early-camp exit habit review for a distance striker.

instructions: Find your most common exit after landing cleanly.
Spot one moment where you remain in range too long.
Choose the safer exit side for that moment.
Write one exit rule you can apply without thinking.
progress: Rehearse the exit rule after every clean score in shadow or technical work.

name: Intercept the Entry
why: Stop pressure before it reaches the pocket and takes away your preferred range.

mindset.intent: Meet the entry before it becomes an exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch the first committed step, dip, load or feint before pressure arrives.
mindset.reset: After the intercept, leave and rebuild the range immediately.
mindset.anchor: Make the entry pay before it gets close.
mindset.context: Opponent-specific entry control for a distance striker.

instructions: Identify the movement that most reliably starts the opponent's entry.
Choose one intercepting action for that trigger.
Choose the exit direction immediately after the intercept.
Define the position or distance you want to reset to.
progress: Rehearse trigger, intercept, exit and reset as one sequence.

name: Exit Lane Audit
why: Choose exits that move away from the opponent's strongest pursuit and return fire.

mindset.intent: Leave through the lane that keeps the next exchange yours.
mindset.focus: Track which direction the opponent follows fastest after you score.
mindset.reset: If the lane closes, protect first and take the next clear exit.
mindset.anchor: Do not exit into their best side.
mindset.context: SPP exit planning against the expected opponent pattern.

instructions: Choose the best exit after your jab.
Choose the best exit after your rear-hand score.
Choose the safest escape when the opponent is already pressuring.
Name the direction you should avoid because it feeds their strongest attack.
progress: Use the exit choices in technical rounds and note which lane stays open most often.

name: Rope and Corner Escape
why: Prepare a calm escape when pressure removes the open space you normally rely on.

mindset.intent: Escape before the position becomes a prolonged pocket exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch which side gets blocked first when the opponent closes the ring.
mindset.reset: Protect, create one lane, then restore long range.
mindset.anchor: One clean exit is enough.
mindset.context: SPP trapped-position planning for a distance striker.

instructions: Identify the moment the ropes or corner begin limiting your movement.
Choose the first defensive action that buys the escape.
Choose the route you will take out of the trapped position.
Define the range you want once you are clear.
progress: Start one technical round near the ropes and rehearse the same escape route.

name: First-Round Range Script
why: Confirm the opening range plan without adding new tactical information late in camp.

mindset.intent: Start simple and establish your distance early.
mindset.focus: Keep only cues you have already trained.
mindset.reset: If the opening gets messy, return to the jab and your preferred range.
mindset.anchor: Simple first, sharp second.
mindset.context: Fight-week confirmation for a distance striker.

instructions: Choose the familiar weapon you will show first.
Choose the first range test you will use to read the opponent.
Confirm your trained response if they rush the space.
Write one short first-round range cue.
progress: Rehearse the cue once in shadow work, then leave it alone.

name: Final Range Cue
why: Reduce your trained range plan to one cue you can recall under pressure.

mindset.intent: Carry one trusted range behaviour into fight day.
mindset.focus: Use only what already worked in camp.
mindset.reset: Return to the same cue after any messy exchange.
mindset.anchor: Range first.
mindset.context: Final taper compression for a distance striker.

instructions: Review one familiar clip or one successful technical round.
Choose the single range behaviour that mattered most.
Turn it into a cue of no more than six words.
progress: Use the same cue in the final light rehearsal; do not add another.

name: Pressure Route Scan
why: Learn where opponents naturally retreat so pressure can steer instead of chase.

mindset.intent: Guide the opponent toward the space you want.
mindset.focus: Watch the first direction they choose when space disappears.
mindset.reset: If you start following, pause and rebuild the angle.
mindset.anchor: Cut the ring, do not chase it.
mindset.context: Early-camp pressure route study for a brawler.

instructions: Identify the opponent's preferred retreat direction.
Choose the direction you should step to cut that route.
Identify the cue that tells you pressure should start.
Choose the area of the ring you want to trap them in.
progress: Use one technical round to steer toward the chosen trap instead of following.

name: Safe Entry Builder
why: Build a repeatable way into the pocket without walking onto clean shots.

mindset.intent: Arrive protected before trying to win the exchange.
mindset.focus: Watch what the opponent throws as someone closes distance.
mindset.reset: If the entry is naked, leave and rebuild the setup.
mindset.anchor: Earn the pocket.
mindset.context: Early-camp entry quality for a brawler.

instructions: Choose the setup that hides your forward step.
Choose the guard position you need while crossing range.
Choose the first punch that establishes the pocket.
Define where your head should finish after the entry.
progress: Rehearse the same setup and head position before adding longer combinations.

name: Pressure Reset
why: Keep pressure controlled so forward intent does not turn into reckless chasing.

mindset.intent: Stay dangerous without becoming hurried.
mindset.focus: Spot the moment your feet begin following instead of cutting.
mindset.reset: Pause the chase, square the stance and rebuild the entry.
mindset.anchor: Pressure is position, not speed.
mindset.context: Early-camp pressure discipline for a brawler.

instructions: Find one sign that your pressure has become rushed.
Choose the safe action that pauses the chase without giving up position.
Choose the setup that starts your next entry.
Write one pressure rule that keeps your feet organised.
progress: Use the reset whenever you notice yourself following during technical work.

name: Pocket Exchange Map
why: Know what happens after the first punches so pocket exchanges stay planned rather than chaotic.

mindset.intent: Win the second decision inside the pocket.
mindset.focus: Watch the opponent's response after the first two punches.
mindset.reset: If the exchange loses shape, smother or leave instead of trading blindly.
mindset.anchor: Know the next beat.
mindset.context: SPP pocket planning for a brawler.

instructions: Identify the opponent's most common pocket sequence.
Choose your answer to that sequence.
Choose the finishing shot that best fits the opening.
Decide whether that exchange should end with an exit or a smother.
progress: Rehearse the chosen exchange ending, not just the opening combination.

name: Body Attack Opportunity
why: Find safe body attacks that reward pressure without making the entry predictable.

mindset.intent: Attack the body when the position earns it.
mindset.focus: Watch for high guards, separated elbows and upright posture.
mindset.reset: If the body line closes, go back upstairs rather than forcing it.
mindset.anchor: Open it before you take it.
mindset.context: SPP body-attack selection for a brawler.

instructions: Identify the clearest body opening the opponent gives away.
Choose the punch or feint that creates that opening.
Choose the body target you will attack.
Choose the head follow-up that punishes their reaction.
progress: Use the body attack only after the chosen setup appears in technical work.

name: Smother and Reset
why: Stop the opponent firing back immediately after your pressure combination lands.

mindset.intent: Own the space after your combination as well as during it.
mindset.focus: Watch when the opponent begins their return fire.
mindset.reset: Close the return, then rebuild before attacking again.
mindset.anchor: Finish safe before restarting.
mindset.context: SPP post-combination control for a brawler.

instructions: Choose where your body should finish after the combination.
Choose your response if the opponent fires back immediately.
Define the smother or control position you can reach safely.
Choose the action that resets you for the next pressure sequence.
progress: Finish every rehearsed combination with the same smother-or-reset decision.

name: First-Round Pressure Script
why: Confirm controlled opening pressure without turning fight-night energy into a reckless start.

mindset.intent: Take space calmly before increasing the exchange rate.
mindset.focus: Use only the pressure actions already rehearsed in camp.
mindset.reset: If you rush, rebuild the ring cut before throwing again.
mindset.anchor: Close calmly.
mindset.context: Fight-week opening script for a brawler.

instructions: Choose the opening pressure action you already trust.
Choose the first ring cut you want to establish.
Choose the first familiar combination you will show.
Write one reset cue that prevents chasing.
progress: Rehearse the script once at low intensity and keep it unchanged.

name: Final Pressure Cue
why: Reduce your pressure plan to one familiar instruction that keeps aggression organised.

mindset.intent: Carry controlled forward pressure into the fight.
mindset.focus: Keep the cue tied to positioning, not emotion.
mindset.reset: Return to the same cue whenever the pace becomes messy.
mindset.anchor: Position before volume.
mindset.context: Final taper compression for a brawler.

instructions: Review one successful pressure sequence from camp.
Choose the behaviour that made the pressure work.
Turn it into one cue of no more than six words.
progress: Use the same cue in the final light rehearsal and do not add another.

name: Trigger Library
why: Build a clear library of movements that reliably predict an opponent's attack.

mindset.intent: Read what happens before the punch, not after it lands.
mindset.focus: Watch shoulders, weight shifts, feet and repeated rhythm changes.
mindset.reset: If the signal is unclear, observe again instead of guessing.
mindset.anchor: Read the trigger first.
mindset.context: Early-camp pattern recognition for a counter striker.

instructions: Identify the clearest signal before a jab.
Identify the clearest signal before a rear-hand attack.
Identify the clearest signal before a committed entry.
Choose the one trigger you trust most.
progress: Look only for the most reliable trigger during the next technical round.

name: Draw the Lead
why: Create predictable attacks instead of waiting passively for a counter opportunity.

mindset.intent: Make the opponent give you the attack you want.
mindset.focus: Watch what reliably makes them throw first.
mindset.reset: If the bait gets no reaction, return to neutral and show something else.
mindset.anchor: Invite, read, answer.
mindset.context: Early-camp counter creation for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose one bait or feint that invites a clear attack.
Name the attack you expect that bait to draw.
Choose the counter you will use against it.
Choose the exit that ends the exchange safely.
progress: Rehearse the bait and expected response before increasing speed.

name: Counter Activity Check
why: Keep counter striking active so patience does not become long periods of inactivity.

mindset.intent: Stay responsible for creating information.
mindset.focus: Notice when waiting stops producing useful reads.
mindset.reset: Use a safe probe when the exchange goes quiet.
mindset.anchor: Patient does not mean passive.
mindset.context: Early-camp activity control for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose one safe action that gathers information without overcommitting.
Find one moment where you waited too long to create a reaction.
Choose the action you can use to provoke a response.
Write one activity rule that keeps you engaged without forcing exchanges.
progress: Use the activity rule during quiet moments in the next technical session.

name: First Beat or Second Beat
why: Decide whether the opponent is safest to counter immediately or after they continue attacking.

mindset.intent: Counter at the beat that leaves the clearest opening.
mindset.focus: Watch whether balance and guard worsen after the first attack.
mindset.reset: If the timing is unclear, defend first and wait for the next clean read.
mindset.anchor: Choose the beat, do not rush it.
mindset.context: SPP timing selection for a counter striker.

instructions: Define when you should counter on the opponent's first attack.
Define when you should wait for their second action instead.
Choose the counter that best fits the clearer beat.
Write the safety rule that tells you when not to fire.
progress: Rehearse both beats, then keep the one that gives the cleaner exit.

name: Counter and Exit
why: Stop a successful counter from becoming a second exchange you did not choose.

mindset.intent: Treat the exit as part of the counter.
mindset.focus: Watch the opponent's first reaction after they are countered.
mindset.reset: Leave before judging how clean the counter landed.
mindset.anchor: Counter, leave, see again.
mindset.context: SPP post-counter positioning for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose the counter you expect to use most often.
Choose the exit direction that avoids the likely return.
Choose the guard position you need while leaving.
Define the distance you want before looking to counter again.
progress: Attach the same exit to the counter every time you rehearse it.

name: Counter the Counter
why: Prepare for the opponent changing their attack after your first counter starts working.

mindset.intent: Expect adaptation instead of assuming the first answer stays open.
mindset.focus: Watch what changes after the opponent has been countered once or twice.
mindset.reset: Abort if the expected adjustment does not appear.
mindset.anchor: Have an answer to their answer.
mindset.context: SPP second-order adjustment for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose the first counter you expect to establish.
Predict the most likely adjustment the opponent makes to avoid it.
Choose your second answer to that adjustment.
Define the cue that tells you to abort rather than force the sequence.
progress: Rehearse the first counter, the likely adjustment and the second answer as one decision chain.

name: First-Round Patience Script
why: Confirm active patience so the opening round gathers information without becoming passive.

mindset.intent: Create reads early without forcing the counter.
mindset.focus: Use only the baits and counters already proven in camp.
mindset.reset: If nothing appears, probe again instead of waiting empty-handed.
mindset.anchor: Active patience.
mindset.context: Fight-week opening script for a counter striker.

instructions: Choose the first safe action you will use to gather information.
Choose one familiar bait that can draw a reaction.
Confirm the counter you already trust most.
Write one activity cue that prevents passive waiting.
progress: Run the opening script once in light rehearsal and keep it unchanged.

name: Final Counter Cue
why: Reduce your counter plan to one familiar read-and-response cue for fight day.

mindset.intent: Trust the read you have already trained.
mindset.focus: Keep one trigger and one response in mind.
mindset.reset: Return to observation if the trigger is not there.
mindset.anchor: See it, answer it.
mindset.context: Final taper compression for a counter striker.

instructions: Review one successful counter sequence from camp.
Choose the trigger you recognised most reliably.
Turn the trigger and response into one cue of no more than six words.
progress: Use the same cue in the final light rehearsal; do not add another counter idea.

name: Opponent Pattern Scan
why: Build basic tactical awareness by separating repeated patterns from one-off moments.

mindset.intent: Look for repetition before making a conclusion.
mindset.focus: Track the same behaviour across several exchanges.
mindset.reset: If the pattern appears once, keep watching before acting on it.
mindset.anchor: Repeated beats random.
mindset.context: General early-camp pattern study.

instructions: Identify the most repeated movement or exchange pattern.
Choose the clearest opportunity that pattern creates.
Choose the main danger linked to that pattern.
Write one observation to test in training rather than treating it as fact.
progress: Test the observation in technical work and keep it only if it repeats.

name: Threat Priority
why: Separate the biggest tactical problem from smaller threats so training attention stays clear.

mindset.intent: Solve the highest-value problem first.
mindset.focus: Rank threats by how often and how badly they change exchanges.
mindset.reset: If everything looks dangerous, return to frequency and consequence.
mindset.anchor: One priority first.
mindset.context: General early-camp threat ranking.

instructions: List the three threats that affect exchanges most often.
Rank them from highest to lowest priority.
Choose the first answer you will train for the top threat.
progress: Build the next tactical rehearsal around the top-ranked threat only.

name: Defensive Habit Review
why: Identify the defensive habit that restores control and the one that keeps you under pressure.

mindset.intent: See what your defence leads to, not just whether it avoids one shot.
mindset.focus: Watch the position immediately after each defensive action.
mindset.reset: Return to the defensive action that gives you sight and balance.
mindset.anchor: Defend into control.
mindset.context: General early-camp defensive habit study.

instructions: Identify your first defensive reaction under pressure.
Find the defensive habit that repeatedly leaves you in a worse position.
Choose the defensive position that restores control best.
Write one defensive rule to carry into technical work.
progress: Use the defensive rule during the next controlled pressure round.

name: Rhythm Map
why: Recognise when exchanges speed up, slow down or become predictable before adding tactics.

mindset.intent: See the tempo changes that organise the fight.
mindset.focus: Notice what happens just before the pace changes.
mindset.reset: If the rhythm becomes unclear, watch one full minute without making notes.
mindset.anchor: Tempo tells you what is next.
mindset.context: General early-camp rhythm study.

instructions: Mark one period where the pace is slow and controlled.
Mark one period where the pace suddenly rises.
Identify what usually causes the change in tempo.
Choose one rhythm you want to impose in training.
progress: Use one technical round to deliberately create the chosen rhythm.

name: First-Exchange Audit
why: Understand what repeatedly decides the first meaningful exchange before longer sequences develop.

mindset.intent: Learn what gives one fighter early control.
mindset.focus: Watch the first committed exchange after each reset.
mindset.reset: Ignore the result and look again at how the exchange started.
mindset.anchor: The start shapes the rest.
mindset.context: General early-camp opening-exchange study.

instructions: Find three first exchanges after clean resets.
Identify what action gave one fighter the advantage most often.
Identify the position that usually followed that advantage.
Choose one opening behaviour to test in training.
progress: Start three technical rounds by testing the chosen opening behaviour.

name: Position Map
why: Identify the positions where you make good decisions and the positions that create rushed choices.

mindset.intent: Know where the fight becomes easiest to read.
mindset.focus: Compare decision quality across different ring or cage positions.
mindset.reset: If a position is unclear, track what happens for the next two exchanges.
mindset.anchor: Good position buys good decisions.
mindset.context: General early-camp position study.

instructions: Choose one position where you consistently make clear decisions.
Choose one position where decisions become rushed or limited.
Identify what movement usually takes you from the bad position to the good one.
Write one positional rule to test.
progress: Use the positional rule in one controlled round and review whether it improves decision quality.

name: Reset Habit Review
why: Make the reset between exchanges deliberate instead of letting the next exchange start from disorder.

mindset.intent: Finish each exchange ready for the next one.
mindset.focus: Watch feet, guard and eyes during the reset.
mindset.reset: If one piece is missing, rebuild it before re-engaging.
mindset.anchor: Reset before restart.
mindset.context: General early-camp reset quality.

instructions: Identify the first thing you normally do after an exchange ends.
Find the part of your stance, guard or vision that is slowest to recover.
Choose the order you want your reset to happen in.
Write one short reset routine.
progress: Use the reset routine after every exchange in the next technical session.

name: Output Window Review
why: Find out when you actually work in a round instead of assuming your output is evenly spread.

mindset.intent: Know when you are working and when you are only watching.
mindset.focus: Track the moments output starts, stops and never restarts.
mindset.reset: When a quiet stretch runs long, restart with the simplest thing you own.
mindset.anchor: Silence is a decision too.
mindset.context: Early-camp work-rate study from your own footage.

instructions: Mark the point in a round where your output is highest.
Mark the longest stretch where you throw nothing at all.
Name what usually ends that quiet stretch.
Write one restart action you can use before the quiet stretch gets long.
progress: Use the restart action in the next rounds you do and note whether the quiet stretches shorten.

name: Stance and Angle Audit
why: Expose the movement direction you default to and the side of the ring or cage you keep giving away.

mindset.intent: Move on purpose rather than out of habit.
mindset.focus: Track which way your feet take you after every exchange.
mindset.reset: If you drift, square up and re-choose the direction before moving again.
mindset.anchor: Pick the angle before it picks you.
mindset.context: Early-camp movement-habit study from your own footage.

instructions: Identify the direction you circle in most often.
Identify the direction you almost never use.
Find the moment your stance stops being usable while you move.
Write one movement rule that forces you to use the neglected direction.
progress: Apply the movement rule in shadow and footwork work; keep it only if your stance stays usable.

name: Fatigue Signature Review
why: Know exactly which part of your technique fails first when you tire, so you can defend it under pressure.

mindset.intent: Protect the thing that breaks first.
mindset.focus: Compare the same action early in a round and late in a round.
mindset.reset: When the flagged fault appears, fix that one thing before anything else.
mindset.anchor: Tired is a technique problem before it is a fitness problem.
mindset.context: Early-camp fatigue study from your own late-round footage.

instructions: Pick one action you use constantly and compare it early and late in a round.
Name the first part of it that degrades when you tire.
Name what that degradation costs you defensively.
Write one cue that holds that part together late in a round.
progress: Use the cue in the last round of your next hard session and note whether the fault still appears.

name: Trigger-Response Builder
why: Turn one reliable opponent signal into a trained action instead of a vague tactical idea.

mindset.intent: Make one read immediately actionable.
mindset.focus: Choose a trigger you can genuinely see in real time.
mindset.reset: If the trigger is absent, stay neutral rather than forcing the response.
mindset.anchor: See it, do it.
mindset.context: General SPP trigger-response work.

instructions: Choose one reliable visual or positional trigger.
Choose the action you will take when it appears.
Choose how you leave after the action.
Choose what you use to reset before the next exchange.
progress: Rehearse the full trigger-response-exit-reset chain in technical work.

name: Round Flow Map
why: Understand how the opponent's behaviour changes through the round instead of treating every minute the same.

mindset.intent: Match your tactical decisions to the part of the round you are in.
mindset.focus: Compare the first, middle and final minute.
mindset.reset: If the pattern changes, update the map rather than forcing the first read.
mindset.anchor: The round has phases too.
mindset.context: General SPP round-management study.

instructions: Describe the opponent's behaviour in the first minute.
Describe what changes in the middle of the round.
Describe what changes in the final minute.
Choose the part of the round where you should take the most control.
progress: Plan one technical round around the chosen control window.

name: Scoring Map
why: Separate clean, repeatable scoring actions from busy work that looks active but gives little return.

mindset.intent: Build around actions that score clearly and leave you organised.
mindset.focus: Watch which actions land cleanly without costing position.
mindset.reset: If an action creates noise but no clean score, move on from it.
mindset.anchor: Repeat what scores cleanly.
mindset.context: General SPP scoring efficiency.

instructions: Choose the cleanest scoring action you can repeat.
Choose the position you want to control while scoring.
Choose one combination worth repeating.
Identify one busy but low-value action to reduce.
progress: Track how often the selected scoring action lands cleanly in technical work.

name: Momentum Shift Review
why: Recognise the moment control changes so you can respond before a bad spell becomes a lost round.

mindset.intent: Notice momentum early enough to act on it.
mindset.focus: Find the exchange or positional change that altered the round.
mindset.reset: Return to the last action that gave you control.
mindset.anchor: Catch the shift early.
mindset.context: General SPP momentum management.

instructions: Find the moment the round clearly changed direction.
Identify what caused the change.
Identify what the fighter gaining control noticed or exploited.
Choose the response you would use to stop the same shift.
progress: Rehearse the chosen response immediately after a deliberately difficult exchange.

name: Adversity Reset
why: Prepare a simple route back to control after being hit, trapped, tired or frustrated.

mindset.intent: Make the first action after adversity predictable and safe.
mindset.focus: Watch what successful fighters do in the first few seconds after trouble.
mindset.reset: Use the same short reset instead of solving everything at once.
mindset.anchor: First get safe, then regain control.
mindset.context: General SPP adversity planning.

instructions: Choose the immediate defensive action you use first after trouble.
Choose one short reset phrase.
Choose the next safe action that restarts your offence or position.
Choose the route that brings you back to control.
progress: Start one technical drill from a disadvantaged position and use the same reset sequence.

name: Adjustment Tree
why: Prepare one clear adjustment when the first tactical plan stops working.

mindset.intent: Change one variable instead of abandoning the whole plan.
mindset.focus: Identify exactly what is failing before choosing the adjustment.
mindset.reset: Keep the parts of the plan that are still working.
mindset.anchor: Adjust, do not panic-rewrite.
mindset.context: General SPP plan-B preparation.

instructions: Name the part of your first plan most likely to fail.
Choose the part that should stay unchanged.
Choose one tactical change that addresses the failure.
Define the sign that tells you the adjustment is working.
progress: Run one technical round where the first option is deliberately removed and use the adjustment.

name: Opening Exchange Test
why: Use the first exchanges to gather specific information instead of trying to prove the whole game plan immediately.

mindset.intent: Make the opening exchange answer one question.
mindset.focus: Choose what you need to learn first about the opponent.
mindset.reset: After the test, return to your base position before changing anything.
mindset.anchor: Test, read, then decide.
mindset.context: General SPP opening-information plan.

instructions: Choose the first tactical question you need answered.
Choose the safe action that tests that question.
Define the response that confirms your read.
Choose what you will do next if the read is confirmed.
progress: Start a technical round with the same test and act only on the observed response.

name: Route to Control
why: Link one difficult position to the position where your decisions and scoring are strongest.

mindset.intent: Know the route back to your best fighting position.
mindset.focus: Watch the movement that changes a bad position into a useful one.
mindset.reset: If the first route is blocked, protect position before trying again.
mindset.anchor: Move toward control.
mindset.context: General SPP positional transition planning.

instructions: Choose the position you most want to avoid staying in.
Choose the position where you perform best.
Identify the movement or action that links the two.
Choose one cue that starts that transition.
progress: Begin one technical drill in the difficult position and earn the route back to control.

name: Last-Minute Control
why: Plan how to close a round clearly when fatigue and urgency make decision-making noisier.

mindset.intent: Finish the round with clear control rather than random volume.
mindset.focus: Watch what changes in the final minute when both fighters know time is short.
mindset.reset: If the finish becomes reckless, return to the safest scoring action.
mindset.anchor: Close clearly.
mindset.context: General SPP final-minute management.

instructions: Identify the safest scoring action late in the round.
Choose the position you want before the final exchange.
Choose the mistake you must avoid when urgency rises.
Write one final-minute instruction.
progress: Finish one technical round using the same final-minute instruction.

name: Corner Instruction Translation
why: Turn a complicated tactical instruction into one action you can execute under fatigue.

mindset.intent: Make the instruction observable and executable.
mindset.focus: Separate what you need to notice from what you need to do.
mindset.reset: If the instruction feels crowded, reduce it to the first action only.
mindset.anchor: One instruction, one action.
mindset.context: General SPP corner-message rehearsal.

instructions: Write the full tactical instruction you want to remember.
Identify the thing you must notice before acting.
Choose the single action that follows that read.
Compress the instruction to three words.
progress: Use only the three-word version during the next hard technical round.

name: Familiar Round-One Rehearsal
why: Confirm a familiar opening sequence without adding new decisions during taper.

mindset.intent: Start with what has already worked in camp.
mindset.focus: Use only confirmed actions and responses.
mindset.reset: If the opening changes, return to the safest familiar action.
mindset.anchor: Familiar first.
mindset.context: General fight-week opening rehearsal.

instructions: Choose the first familiar action you will show.
Choose the response you already trust if the opponent disrupts it.
Choose the position you want after the opening exchange.
Say the sequence once in plain language.
progress: Rehearse the sequence once at low intensity, then stop analysing it.

name: Final Tactical Cue Card
why: Reduce the trained game plan to a few familiar cues that remain usable under pressure.

mindset.intent: Carry only the most useful information into fight day.
mindset.focus: Use cues already rehearsed successfully.
mindset.reset: If thoughts multiply, return to the single final sentence.
mindset.anchor: Simple survives pressure.
mindset.context: Final fight-week tactical compression.

instructions: Choose one familiar entry cue.
Choose one familiar scoring cue.
Choose one danger cue and one reset phrase.
Condense them into one final sentence you can recall under pressure.
progress: Read the final sentence before the last light rehearsal; add nothing new.

name: Trained Response Confirmation
why: Confirm the two responses you have the most repetitions in and drop everything you have not trained.

mindset.intent: Go in with the answers you already own.
mindset.focus: Look only at work you have repeated successfully in camp.
mindset.reset: If you start weighing options, go back to the response with the most repetitions.
mindset.anchor: Trained beats clever.
mindset.context: Fight-week confirmation of already-trained responses.

instructions: List the two responses you have repeated most often this camp.
Confirm the situation each one belongs to.
Remove any response you have not trained enough to trust.
Say both responses out loud in the situation they belong to.
progress: Confirm both in light shadow work only; add no new response this week.

name: Familiar Threat Rehearsal
why: Rehearse the answer you have already trained for the danger you already know about, without adding new theory.

mindset.intent: Meet the known danger with a known answer.
mindset.focus: Watch only footage of the threat you have already prepared for.
mindset.reset: If the answer feels unclear, use the simpler version you have trained more.
mindset.anchor: Known danger, known answer.
mindset.context: Fight-week rehearsal of an already-prepared threat.

instructions: Name the one danger you have prepared for most in this camp.
Name the trained answer that goes with it.
Confirm the position you want to be in immediately after using it.
Rehearse the answer slowly until it needs no thought.
progress: Rehearse it once more at low intensity before fight day and leave the rest alone.

name: Cage Route Scan (MMA)
why: Learn the opponent's first escape route when forward pressure closes open space.

mindset.intent: Deny the preferred cage exit without following it in a straight line.
mindset.focus: First circle, reversal, frame, level change or clinch as the fence nears.
mindset.reset: If the route is unreadable, square the stance at safe striking range and rebuild the cut.
mindset.anchor: Close the door; do not chase the runner.
mindset.context: Finish outside the opponent's lead shoulder with the fence still limiting their next exit.

instructions: Record the direction of the opponent's first two exits as their back approaches the fence.
Identify whether footwork, a frame, a level change or a clinch creates each escape.
Choose the step and angle that blocks the preferred route while preserving stance and shot defence.
progress: During the next technical round, verify whether the predicted first exit appears twice.

name: Level-Threat Pressure Map (MMA)
why: Find the moments when striking pressure makes a wrestling threat believable.

mindset.intent: Connect only when the opponent's reaction improves the level change or clinch entry.
mindset.focus: A widened stance, raised guard, shell or upright retreat after a strike or feint.
mindset.reset: If hips are back, feet are crossed or distance is stretched, stay upright and recover position.
mindset.anchor: Pressure creates the shot; position authorises it.
mindset.context: Finish chest-to-hip, on a secure body lock or back at organised striking pressure.

instructions: Name the strike or feint that changes the opponent's stance or guard most reliably.
Match each reaction to level change, clinch connection or continued striking.
Mark one poor-position cue that cancels the entry before commitment.
progress: Test one mapped reaction in drilling and confirm that the chosen connection arrives balanced.

name: Pressure Reset (MMA)
why: Recognise the exact point where organised pressure turns into exposed chasing.

mindset.intent: Restore stance before trying to win the lost ground again.
mindset.focus: Head over the lead knee, crossed feet, reaching posture or an opponent suddenly gaining a clean angle.
mindset.reset: Plant under the hips, bring the rear foot back into base and restart behind a familiar feint.
mindset.anchor: Base first, pressure second.
mindset.context: Finish square to the opponent with both defensive reactions available.

instructions: Identify which opponent escape most often tempts the athlete to overrun the stance.
Freeze the footage at the first posture or foot-position error, not after the counter lands.
Select one two-step positional reset and the familiar action that restarts controlled pressure.
progress: Use the reset once in a pressure round before adding any new offence.

name: Strike-to-Fence Decision (MMA)
why: Decide whether an opponent-specific strike reaction calls for more striking, fence connection or release.

mindset.intent: Take the branch that produces effective offence instead of forcing every exchange to the fence.
mindset.focus: Their guard return, hip position and exit line immediately after the selected entry strike.
mindset.reset: If neither clean follow-up nor secure connection exists, angle out before the counter or shot.
mindset.anchor: Read the reaction, then choose the phase.
mindset.context: Finish with a clean second strike, connected fence position or a protected disengagement.

instructions: Study the expected opponent's response to the exact strike planned for closing distance.
Label one response for continued striking and a different response for clinch-to-fence connection.
Add the response that demands disengagement, including the safe exit direction.
progress: Rehearse the three-way branch until the correct finish can be called before the second action.

name: Cage Re-Catch (MMA)
why: Map the second cut after the expected opponent escapes the first cage trap.

mindset.intent: Arrive at the next lane before their direction change rather than sprinting behind them.
mindset.focus: Whether the opponent continues circling, reverses direction or attacks immediately after clearing the fence.
mindset.reset: If the re-catch line exposes the hips or centreline, hold centre and restart the cut.
mindset.anchor: Win the second corner, not the foot race.
mindset.context: Finish intercepting the next escape lane with stance intact and the opponent still outside centre.

instructions: Track the expected opponent's exit direction from the first fence exchange.
Note their second movement once open space appears: continue, reverse or counter forward.
Place the second cut where that movement will arrive and name the shot or counter cue that cancels pursuit.
progress: In situational work, score a re-catch only when the second cut happens without crossed feet.

name: Fence Escape Denial (MMA)
why: Identify the expected opponent's preferred technical escape from fence control and its direct denial.

mindset.intent: Answer the escape mechanism before adding offence from the clinch.
mindset.focus: Their underhook or pummel, turn, frame, level change or disengagement attempt.
mindset.reset: If inside position is lost completely, release safely and re-square instead of clinging to weak control.
mindset.anchor: Deny the escape that is actually happening.
mindset.context: Finish with restored head-and-hand position, a clean turn or effective offence from stable control.

instructions: Classify the opponent's most common fence escape by hands, hips and head position.
Choose one denial specific to that escape and state which side must remain closed.
Define the strike, takedown or positional advance available only after control is restored.
progress: Review the next fence round for successful denials, not total time spent holding position.

name: First Pressure Sequence (MMA)
why: Compress the opening pressure plan to one trained cue and one trusted sequence.

mindset.intent: Start composed and let the familiar cue release the opening attack.
mindset.focus: The rehearsed stance or first-step cue that exposes the opponent's preferred cage route.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: the feet narrow or the opponent changes level; re-square and return to the opening feint.
mindset.anchor: See the first step. Take the first lane.
mindset.context: Finish the sequence balanced at the fence line or safely back in centre control.

instructions: Name the single familiar cue that starts the planned pressure sequence.
Visualise the exact strike-and-cut response and its intended finishing position.
Rehearse the danger cue once, followed immediately by the trained stance reset.
progress: Carry only this opening sequence into fight week; add no new branch.

name: Final Pressure Rule (MMA)
why: Keep one final rule that prevents pressure from becoming reckless pursuit.

mindset.intent: Advance only while stance and defensive responsibility remain organised.
mindset.focus: The familiar cue that confirms the opponent is still contained rather than escaping on an angle.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: reaching past the lead knee; stop, rebuild base and restart behind the trusted action.
mindset.anchor: Contained, balanced, dangerous.
mindset.context: Finish every pressure exchange able to strike, defend a shot or disengage.

instructions: State the one cue that permits another forward step.
Pair it with the single familiar response already rehearsed in camp.
Say the danger cue and positional reset aloud before ending the review.
progress: Use the rule as the final corner reminder, without expanding the plan.

name: Attack Trigger Map (MMA)
why: Build a library of the opponent's initiating cues before choosing any counter.

mindset.intent: Read the start of the attack rather than reacting to impact.
mindset.focus: Lead-foot load, shoulder twitch, hand drop, level dip or stance switch that precedes offence.
mindset.reset: If the cue is ambiguous, keep the guard and angle away instead of guessing a counter.
mindset.anchor: Counter the launch, not the noise.
mindset.context: Finish outside the attacking line with vision and stance preserved.

instructions: Find three attacks and rewind to the earliest repeatable movement before each one.
Separate cues for punches, kicks, entries and level changes.
Rank the cues by reliability and choose only the clearest for training.
progress: Call the attack correctly from the cue in three fresh clips before progressing.

name: Safe Counter Range (MMA)
why: Distinguish counter range from the distance where a counter becomes a clinch or takedown risk.

mindset.intent: Counter only from a range that leaves a defendable second beat.
mindset.focus: The opponent's step depth and whether their hips or shoulders enter after the strike.
mindset.reset: If they crash through the counter line, frame, pummel or angle clear instead of admiring the shot.
mindset.anchor: Score with room for the next phase.
mindset.context: Finish beyond their follow-up strike or in deliberate inside control.

instructions: Pause examples at the moment the first attack enters range and mark both athletes' feet.
Decide which counters retain space and which invite immediate body contact.
Assign an exit or connection response to each range before reviewing the result.
progress: Confirm in technical work that the counter leaves a reliable defensive second action.

name: Counter Exit or Connection (MMA)
why: Recognise when a landed counter should end with an angle and when it should become grappling contact.

mindset.intent: Choose the finish from the opponent's forward momentum after the counter.
mindset.focus: Whether their feet stop, posture folds forward or hips continue driving into range.
mindset.reset: If balance is unclear, post and circle to open space before adding offence.
mindset.anchor: Exit stopped pressure; connect through continuing pressure.
mindset.context: Finish at a clean outside angle or with secure head-and-hand contact.

instructions: Compare counters that halt the opponent with counters they absorb while still advancing.
For a stopped opponent, name the safe exit lane; for continued drive, name the connection.
Reject any follow-up that leaves the athlete square with no answer to the next phase.
progress: Review the next counter round for correct finishes after both reactions.

name: Counter-to-Takedown Decision (MMA)
why: Identify which expected striking reaction exposes a takedown after the counter lands.

mindset.intent: Change levels only when the counter fixes posture or stance in the planned direction.
mindset.focus: A high guard, squared feet or forward recovery step after the chosen counter.
mindset.reset: If the opponent retracts hips or regains angle, take the strike and exit rather than forcing the shot.
mindset.anchor: The counter earns the entry; the feet confirm it.
mindset.context: Finish connected below the hips or safely outside the return attack.

instructions: Study the expected opponent's recovery after the exact counter selected for camp.
Mark the recovery that creates hip access and the recovery that removes it.
Build a two-branch rule: connect on the exposed stance, exit on the recovered stance.
progress: Test both opponent reactions in constrained drilling without adding a third option.

name: Counter After Level Change (MMA)
why: Punish the expected opponent's level-change entry without confusing it with a failed-shot scramble.

mindset.intent: Defend the entry first, then strike during their posture recovery.
mindset.focus: Head position, lead knee and reaching hands as they change level from striking range.
mindset.reset: If hip control is not secure, frame and circle before attempting the return strike.
mindset.anchor: Stop the entry, find the head, leave the line.
mindset.context: Finish upright at an angle after a legal strike or with dominant front-head position.

instructions: Identify the opponent's preferred level-change setup and the first defensive contact it requires.
Locate the brief window when their head rises or hands separate after the defence.
Choose one legal return and the angle that avoids their immediate re-shot.
progress: Score the drill only when defence is complete before the counter begins.

name: Punish Failed Shot (MMA)
why: Exploit the moment after the expected opponent's takedown attempt has clearly failed.

mindset.intent: Turn a defended shot into immediate effective offence without surrendering hip safety.
mindset.focus: Their knees, hands and head position as they abandon the finish or rise.
mindset.reset: If they retain a leg or body lock, keep defending and improve position before striking.
mindset.anchor: Failed means cleared; then punish.
mindset.context: Finish with a clean strike, a dominant spin behind or separation on the athlete's terms.

instructions: Separate footage of fully cleared shots from attempts that still retain meaningful control.
Choose the opponent-specific rise or retreat cue that confirms the shot is over.
Match that cue to one high-percentage strike or positional takeover and its safe finish.
progress: Review whether the follow-up begins only after the legs and hips are free.

name: First Counter Trigger (MMA)
why: Reduce the opening counter plan to the opponent's most familiar initiating cue.

mindset.intent: Wait for the rehearsed launch signal and fire the trusted counter.
mindset.focus: The single shoulder, foot or level cue repeatedly seen in preparation.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: the attack shape changes; cover, angle out and return to observation.
mindset.anchor: One launch signal, one answer.
mindset.context: Finish outside the return line with stance ready.

instructions: Name the one opening cue retained from camp analysis.
Visualise the familiar counter and its exact post-counter angle.
Rehearse one false read followed by the practiced defensive reset.
progress: Take only this trigger into the final review.

name: Counter-and-Reset Cue (MMA)
why: Keep the counter plan disciplined by attaching one reset to the trusted response.

mindset.intent: Complete the exit before looking for another counter.
mindset.focus: The familiar impact or posture cue confirming the response has finished.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: staying square for a second exchange; step to the trained outside angle and reframe.
mindset.anchor: Counter complete means position restored.
mindset.context: Finish seeing both hands and the opponent's hips from a stable base.

instructions: Recall the single counter already selected for the matchup.
Attach the exact familiar exit step used after it in camp.
End with the square-stance danger cue and the known angle reset.
progress: Use this as a brief completion reminder, not a new combination study.

name: MMA Range Map (MMA)
why: Separate clean striking range from the distances where kicks, punches, clinches and shots overlap.

mindset.intent: Hold the range that scores while keeping enough space to read phase changes.
mindset.focus: Lead-foot distance plus the opponent's ability to touch the hips without an extra step.
mindset.reset: When ranges collapse, frame or pivot back to the chosen long-range marker.
mindset.anchor: Own the gap between strike and connection.
mindset.context: Finish at long striking range with the centreline and hips protected.

instructions: Mark the distance for the athlete's longest reliable strike in three exchanges.
Mark where the opponent can enter punches, kicks, clinch contact or a shot from one movement.
Define the foot-position cue that keeps the athlete in the useful gap between those zones.
progress: Check the range marker during drilling without adding volume.

name: Exit Before Connection (MMA)
why: Recognise the final beat available to exit before the opponent secures body contact.

mindset.intent: Leave on the entry step rather than after hands reach the torso.
mindset.focus: The opponent's chest crossing over the lead knee while the rear foot drives forward.
mindset.reset: If contact is already made, establish frames and inside position instead of retreating upright.
mindset.anchor: Beat the hands or win the contact.
mindset.context: Finish at an outside angle before connection, or in a stable clinch if the exit was late.

instructions: Find entries where the opponent covers distance with a second committed step.
Freeze the last frame where a lateral exit remains available without crossing feet.
Assign a frame-and-pummel response for every example where that frame has passed.
progress: In technical rounds, grade the timing of the exit rather than total distance travelled.

name: Long-Range Threat Scan (MMA)
why: Identify which long-range weapons deter entry and which invite a level change or catch.

mindset.intent: Select long attacks that preserve balance and hide the next defensive read.
mindset.focus: Opponent reactions to the lead kick, straight strike and feint from outside range.
mindset.reset: If the weapon leaves the stance square or leg available, recover before repeating it.
mindset.anchor: Long offence must return to a defendable stance.
mindset.context: Finish with both hips under control and an exit lane visible.

instructions: Compare how the opponent closes distance after each primary long-range weapon.
Note whether they retreat, parry and return, catch timing or change level underneath.
Choose the weapon whose recovery best answers the most common reaction.
progress: Carry the selected weapon and recovery into one low-volume range round.

name: Intercept the Entry (MMA)
why: Choose an opponent-specific intercept for the first committed step into range.

mindset.intent: Damage or disrupt the entry while preserving the exit from the follow-up phase.
mindset.focus: The expected opponent's lead-foot landing and head line during their preferred entry.
mindset.reset: If the intercept does not stop momentum, frame and angle rather than throwing in place.
mindset.anchor: Intercept, assess momentum, leave.
mindset.context: Finish outside their second step or in deliberate contact with head position.

instructions: Study the exact entry pattern expected in the matchup and identify its committed first step.
Select one intercept that lands before their hands or hips establish control.
Add a branch for stopped momentum and a branch for continued forward drive.
progress: Rehearse the MMA intercept against the opponent's actual entry rhythm and transition threat.

name: Angle Off Before Fence (MMA)
why: Prevent the expected pressure pattern from carrying the athlete to the cage before the angle is taken.

mindset.intent: Turn while open space remains, not after the back foot meets the boundary.
mindset.focus: The second retreating step and the opponent's shoulder line steering the approach.
mindset.reset: If the fence is already reached, plant, frame and exit through a rehearsed side rather than circling blindly.
mindset.anchor: Angle on step two; do not donate the fence.
mindset.context: Finish facing centre with the opponent forced to turn before attacking again.

instructions: Trace the opponent's pressure route and identify the step that removes the final open lane.
Choose the opponent-specific pivot or lateral step that beats their steering shoulder.
Define the fence-contact contingency when the early angle is missed.
progress: Grade the next pressure drill on exits completed before boundary contact.

name: Takedown-Threat Distance (MMA)
why: Calibrate striking choices around the expected opponent's true takedown launch distance.

mindset.intent: Score without placing both feet inside the opponent's best shot window.
mindset.focus: Their penetration-step reach after the setup they are most likely to use.
mindset.reset: When both feet enter that window, recover one step or present a planned anti-entry frame.
mindset.anchor: Know the shot line before opening the strike line.
mindset.context: Finish every long attack beyond hip contact or prepared to defend it.

instructions: Measure the expected opponent's level-change distance from their preferred setup.
Compare it with the recovery position after the athlete's chosen long strikes.
Remove or modify the strike that repeatedly leaves both feet inside the launch window.
progress: Validate the chosen range against live entry attempts at controlled pace.

name: First-Round Range Script (MMA)
why: Carry one familiar opening range check into the first exchange.

mindset.intent: Establish distance with the trusted long weapon and recover immediately.
mindset.focus: The opponent's first step after the known range-finding action.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: they cover two beats at once; angle out and restore the long-range marker.
mindset.anchor: Touch range, read the step, recover.
mindset.context: Finish the opening exchange in open space with stance intact.

instructions: Name the single familiar action used to establish distance.
Visualise the expected first-step reaction and the trained range response.
Rehearse the two-beat danger cue followed by the known lateral reset.
progress: Keep the script to this one opening read.

name: Preferred Exit Cue (MMA)
why: Lock in the safest familiar exit cue for the final preparation window.

mindset.intent: Leave as soon as the opponent's pressure step closes the chosen buffer.
mindset.focus: The rehearsed lead-foot crossing that signals the outside lane is available.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: the lane closes toward the fence; frame, re-square and use the practiced opposite exit.
mindset.anchor: See the foot, take the lane.
mindset.context: Finish facing centre with the opponent outside the athlete's lead shoulder.

instructions: Recall the one foot-position cue used successfully in camp.
Pair it with the familiar pivot or lateral step, without adding strikes.
End on the boundary danger cue and the opposite-side reset.
progress: Use only this exit reminder in the final technical session.

name: Safe Clinch Entry Map (MMA)
why: Find the entries that reach clinch contact without crossing an unprotected striking or shot line.

mindset.intent: Connect behind a defensive reaction rather than walking in with extended arms.
mindset.focus: Guard closure, elbow separation or planted feet after a strike or feint.
mindset.reset: If the opponent remains square and ready, exit behind the guard and rebuild the setup.
mindset.anchor: Earn contact before controlling it.
mindset.context: Finish forehead-to-temple with inside hand position or safely outside range.

instructions: Compare entries made behind punches, feints and opponent attacks.
Identify the reaction that hides hand connection and head placement most reliably.
Reject any route that exposes the chin or hips before contact is established.
progress: Drill the safest route to first contact without continuing to a finish.

name: Head-and-Hand Position Audit (MMA)
why: Understand how head position, inside control and frames decide the first clinch exchange.

mindset.intent: Win alignment before seeking strikes, turns or takedowns.
mindset.focus: Forehead line, elbow position, underhook depth and the opponent's framing hand.
mindset.reset: If the head slips outside and both hands lose inside space, pummel to neutral before attacking.
mindset.anchor: Head leads; hands secure; hips follow.
mindset.context: Finish with posture aligned and at least one reliable inside control.

instructions: Pause each clinch entry at first contact and mark both head positions.
Identify who owns inside hand space and which frame prevents chest connection.
Choose the smallest pummel or head adjustment that restores attacking alignment.
progress: Audit first-contact position in the next clinch round before counting offence.

name: Clinch Exit Awareness (MMA)
why: Recognise the opponent's preferred route for leaving open-space clinches.

mindset.intent: Release with position or follow the exit only when the next attack is protected.
mindset.focus: Their elbow frame, hip turn, head slip or level change immediately before separation.
mindset.reset: If grips break without posture, cover and re-square instead of reaching to reconnect.
mindset.anchor: Own the break before owning the next beat.
mindset.context: Finish with guard restored and the opponent still in view.

instructions: Catalogue whether the opponent exits by frame, turn, retreat or level change.
Mark the side their head and lead foot travel as contact breaks.
Assign a safe strike, re-clinch or disengagement only after posture is recovered.
progress: Review the next session for clean breaks rather than total clinch duration.

name: Fence Turn Decision (MMA)
why: Choose the opponent-specific moment to reverse fence position instead of holding neutral clinch control.

mindset.intent: Turn when their stance and posting hand remove the base needed to resist.
mindset.focus: Feet becoming parallel, head drifting outside or the far hand posting away from the body.
mindset.reset: If their base stays wide and head position is strong, pummel or strike before forcing the turn.
mindset.anchor: Turn the weak base, not the strong wall.
mindset.context: Finish with the opponent on the fence and immediate effective offence available.

instructions: Study the expected opponent's feet and posting habits during fence clinches.
Identify the exact stance or hand cue that makes the planned turn available.
Choose the follow-up strike, takedown or release that proves the reversal was useful.
progress: Score the sequence only when the turn creates offence rather than a position swap alone.

name: Underhook Battle Map (MMA)
why: Map the expected opponent's pummel response and the next control created by winning or losing the underhook.

mindset.intent: Treat each underhook exchange as a branch, not a prolonged strength contest.
mindset.focus: Elbow height, shoulder pressure and the side the opponent uses to swim inside.
mindset.reset: If the underhook is lost deep, frame the crossface line and recover base before re-pummelling.
mindset.anchor: Win the elbow line or change the problem.
mindset.context: Finish with a usable body lock, head position or safe separation.

instructions: Identify which side the expected opponent prefers for their first underhook.
Map the response when the athlete wins inside space and the response when the opponent wins it.
Attach one offensive continuation to the successful branch and one recovery to the lost branch.
progress: Rehearse both branches from first pummel contact, not from a static winning grip.

name: Clinch Strike or Takedown (MMA)
why: Decide whether the expected clinch reaction is more vulnerable to strikes or a takedown continuation.

mindset.intent: Attack the opening their posture creates instead of defaulting to one phase.
mindset.focus: High upright posture, low braced hips, separated elbows or a hand committed to pummelling.
mindset.reset: If neither strike nor takedown has clean structure, improve head position and reset the decision.
mindset.anchor: Posture tells you what the clinch is giving.
mindset.context: Finish with impactful legal strikes, a takedown to advantage or a protected release.

instructions: Study the expected opponent under the exact head-and-hand control planned for camp.
Assign upright or open-elbow reactions to a strike and over-braced reactions to a takedown route.
Name the neutral reaction that requires positional improvement before either attack.
progress: Run the three-reaction decision from live pummelling at controlled intensity.

name: First Clinch Entry Cue (MMA)
why: Retain one familiar cue for the first safe clinch connection.

mindset.intent: Enter only behind the rehearsed guard or posture reaction.
mindset.focus: The single elbow or head-position opening seen repeatedly in camp.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: the opponent stays square with hips ready; cover and return to the entry setup.
mindset.anchor: One opening, clean contact.
mindset.context: Finish with trusted head position and inside control.

instructions: Name the one reaction that authorises the familiar entry.
Visualise the trained hand connection and head placement.
Rehearse the square-hips danger cue and the known disengagement once.
progress: Keep only this first-contact picture for fight week.

name: One Fence Control Rule (MMA)
why: Compress fence work to one rule that turns control into meaningful offence.

mindset.intent: Maintain the trusted control only while it creates a strike, takedown or advance.
mindset.focus: The familiar head-and-hand position that makes the chosen offence available.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: control becomes static or inside position disappears; release and re-square.
mindset.anchor: Control must pay immediately.
mindset.context: Finish with effective offence or a clean reset away from dead position.

instructions: Recall the single fence position trusted in preparation.
Pair it with the one familiar attack it reliably produces.
Close on the static-control danger cue and the practiced release.
progress: Use the rule as a short reminder, with no new fence sequence.

name: Entry-to-Contact Map (MMA)
why: Map how the athlete reaches meaningful grappling contact through striking danger.

mindset.intent: Arrive at hips or upper-body control with posture protected.
mindset.focus: The opponent's hand position and weight transfer after jabs, kicks or feints.
mindset.reset: If the entry line is uncovered, return to range and rebuild behind a defensive reaction.
mindset.anchor: Safe contact starts before the grip.
mindset.context: Finish connected with head position and feet able to drive or turn.

instructions: Compare level changes, clinch entries and reactive connections from open space.
Identify which setup moves the opponent's hands away from the intended contact point.
Mark the posture cue that makes each route unsafe before commitment.
progress: Drill the highest-quality route only to secure contact and stable base.

name: Takedown Setup Reaction (MMA)
why: Identify the specific opponent reaction that makes a takedown entry available.

mindset.intent: Enter on changed stance or posture, not simply because a setup was thrown.
mindset.focus: Feet squaring, weight rising, elbows lifting or a committed counter after the setup.
mindset.reset: If the reaction does not move stance or posture, reset behind guard without shooting.
mindset.anchor: The reaction opens the takedown.
mindset.context: Finish on connected hips or back at safe setup range.

instructions: Select three familiar strikes or feints and observe the opponent's immediate response.
Choose the response that gives the cleanest head line and hip access.
Write one no-entry cue for the same setup when the opponent remains structurally ready.
progress: Test whether the chosen reaction reliably precedes clean connection in drilling.

name: Ground Destination Map (MMA)
why: Choose the position each takedown should produce instead of treating floor contact as the finish.

mindset.intent: Direct the takedown toward a stable landing that supports immediate offence.
mindset.focus: Opponent stance, fence proximity and likely turn or guard recovery during descent.
mindset.reset: If the planned landing is lost, secure base and prioritise position before striking or submitting.
mindset.anchor: Name the landing before the entry.
mindset.context: Finish past the legs, in strong half guard or another preselected advantageous position.

instructions: Review where each primary takedown actually lands against common stance reactions.
Identify the grip and finishing direction that steer toward the preferred resulting position.
Define the first control needed when the opponent turns and the ideal destination is missed.
progress: Track successful takedowns by resulting position and offence, not by floor contact alone.

name: Fence Finish Decision (MMA)
why: Select the best opponent-specific finish once a takedown entry reaches the fence.

mindset.intent: Change finish when the opponent's base defeats the first direction.
mindset.focus: Their near-side underhook, knee width, hip height and posting foot against the fence.
mindset.reset: If head position or hand connection is lost, rebuild the clinch before driving again.
mindset.anchor: Read the base, finish through its weak side.
mindset.context: Finish in an advantageous ground position with control ready for offence.

instructions: Study the expected opponent's preferred fence defence to the primary takedown.
Match their wide base, underhook or turn to the planned secondary finish.
Specify the head-position loss that pauses the chain and returns to clinch control.
progress: Rehearse the first-to-second finish transition against the actual defensive shape.

name: Chain Attempt Map (MMA)
why: Use the expected defence to the first takedown as the setup for the next attempt.

mindset.intent: Change direction or level while connection and base remain useful.
mindset.focus: The opponent's sprawl, whizzer, step-out or hip turn after the primary entry.
mindset.reset: If both knees collapse or grips separate, recover posture instead of chaining blindly.
mindset.anchor: Their defence names the next attack.
mindset.context: Finish on the secondary takedown or in a stable clinch reset.

instructions: Identify the expected opponent's highest-frequency defence to the primary attempt.
Choose the secondary attack that uses the direction and weight of that defence.
Mark the connection-loss cue that ends the chain before position deteriorates.
progress: Drill the chain from a realistic defended first attempt, not a cooperative pause.

name: Top Control to Effective Offense (MMA)
why: Turn the expected top position into strikes, submission threat or meaningful advancement.

mindset.intent: Use control as the platform for offence rather than the final objective.
mindset.focus: The opponent's framing elbow, hip turn and hand commitment during their first escape.
mindset.reset: If posture or base breaks, re-secure position before forcing damage or a submission.
mindset.anchor: Position earns value through attack.
mindset.context: Finish with clean ground strikes, a credible submission sequence or improved dominant position.

instructions: Start from the likely post-takedown position against the expected opponent.
Identify the first escape reaction that exposes a strike, pass or submission route.
Choose the offensive continuation and the base cue that must remain intact while attacking.
progress: Review the round for productive attacks and advances, not static control time.

name: First Takedown Setup (MMA)
why: Retain one familiar setup for the first takedown attempt.

mindset.intent: Enter only when the trained stance reaction appears.
mindset.focus: The single weight shift or guard lift repeatedly created in camp.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: the opponent's hips withdraw; abandon the entry and return to the setup stance.
mindset.anchor: Create the reaction, then connect.
mindset.context: Finish on stable hip contact or safely back at range.

instructions: Name the one familiar setup retained for fight week.
Visualise the known reaction and the trusted entry behind it.
Rehearse the withdrawn-hips danger cue and the practiced abort once.
progress: Keep the review to this first-attempt picture.

name: First Ground Continuation Cue (MMA)
why: Preload one familiar continuation after the first successful takedown.

mindset.intent: Advance or strike from the opponent's known first ground reaction.
mindset.focus: The single frame, hip turn or get-up post expected on landing.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: base loosens during offence; settle position and rebuild control.
mindset.anchor: Land, read, continue once.
mindset.context: Finish in the trained dominant position with effective offence available.

instructions: Recall the opponent reaction most often seen after the planned takedown.
Pair it with the one familiar strike, pass or submission continuation.
Close on the lost-base danger cue and the known stabilising reset.
progress: Use one short continuation rehearsal and add nothing new.

name: Range Transition Map (MMA)
why: Understand the distances where striking becomes clinch or takedown contact.

mindset.intent: Move between phases deliberately instead of drifting through the transition range.
mindset.focus: The opponent's foot depth and hand position as long range collapses to body contact.
mindset.reset: If the transition arrives without posture or hand position, exit to the last stable range.
mindset.anchor: Cross ranges with a purpose.
mindset.context: Finish in clean striking space, secure clinch contact or connected to the hips.

instructions: Mark long, punching, clinch and shot ranges in repeated exchanges.
Identify the cue that should trigger a deliberate phase change at each boundary.
Name the stable position used when the intended transition is unavailable.
progress: Practice calling the phase before crossing its range line.

name: Best Phase Identification (MMA)
why: Identify where the athlete consistently creates the most effective offence.

mindset.intent: Use other phases to reach the strongest one rather than competing everywhere equally.
mindset.focus: Where strikes land cleanly, positions advance or credible submissions develop.
mindset.reset: When a phase produces only neutral control, return to the route that creates impact or advantage.
mindset.anchor: Transitions serve the winning phase.
mindset.context: Finish in the position that repeatedly produces meaningful offence.

instructions: Review exchanges across open striking, clinch, fence and ground.
Separate activity from results by noting impact, advancement and real finishing threats.
Choose the two most reliable routes into the phase with the best results.
progress: Use the next technical session to confirm one route into the identified winning phase.

name: Strike Clinch or Shot Tree (MMA)
why: Build a simple three-branch decision for the opponent's first defensive reaction.

mindset.intent: Let posture and distance select continued striking, clinch contact or a shot.
mindset.focus: High guard with planted feet, forward collision or hips exposed beneath upright retreat.
mindset.reset: If the reaction is neutral, exit on angle and restart the setup.
mindset.anchor: One reaction, one phase branch.
mindset.context: Finish with effective striking, secure upper-body control or connected hips.

instructions: Choose one familiar initiating strike and list the three most common reactions to it.
Assign each distinct reaction to continued strikes, clinch entry or takedown entry.
Add the neutral read that sends the athlete back to range without commitment.
progress: Drill the tree with randomised reactions until phase choice precedes movement.

name: Strike-to-Shot Branch (MMA)
why: Exploit the expected opponent's defensive striking reaction as the entry to their hips.

mindset.intent: Change level on the planned guard or stance shift, not by preset combination count.
mindset.focus: Their hands rising, feet squaring or weight planting after the selected strike.
mindset.reset: If the hips withdraw or the counter line stays open, finish the strike and angle away.
mindset.anchor: Strike creates posture; posture selects the shot.
mindset.context: Finish connected beneath the hips or beyond the opponent's return attack.

instructions: Study the exact strike selected to draw the expected opponent's defensive response.
Identify which response exposes the shot and which response demands a striking exit.
Define the second decision if the first takedown contact meets their preferred defence.
progress: Rehearse the opponent-specific branch from the strike through first defensive contact.

name: Shot-to-Strike Branch (MMA)
why: Use the expected takedown defence to create a clean striking continuation.

mindset.intent: Return to offence as the opponent rebuilds posture after denying the shot.
mindset.focus: Their head rise, hand separation or square stance when they clear the entry.
mindset.reset: If a leg or body lock remains contested, keep positional responsibility before striking.
mindset.anchor: Clear contact, then strike the recovery.
mindset.context: Finish on a legal strike at an angle or reconnect if their posture collapses forward.

instructions: Map how the expected opponent exits the primary shot defence.
Choose the recovery beat that exposes a specific strike without abandoning control early.
Add the branch where their forward posture makes re-connection safer than striking.
progress: Train the shot-to-strike switch only after a clearly resolved first phase.

name: Winning the Second Phase (MMA)
why: Plan the opponent-specific action that wins after the opening phase changes.

mindset.intent: Treat the transition result as the real scoring opportunity.
mindset.focus: The first stable posture after strike-to-clinch, shot-to-scramble or clinch-to-break.
mindset.reset: If the second phase begins without base, secure position before forcing offence.
mindset.anchor: The second phase completes the first attack.
mindset.context: Finish with impact, positional advancement or a credible finishing threat after transition.

instructions: Select the matchup's most likely first phase and the transition it usually creates.
Identify the opponent reaction that decides who owns the next stable position.
Choose the immediate second-phase action and the cue that delays it for positional safety.
progress: Review complete sequences for who wins after transition, not who initiates first.

name: A/B Opening Plan (MMA)
why: Keep two familiar opening routes tied to one clear opponent reaction.

mindset.intent: Begin with route A and switch to route B only on the trained cue.
mindset.focus: The known stance or guard response that closes the first route and opens the second.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: neither route has structure; reset to centre behind the opening feint.
mindset.anchor: A first; B only on cue.
mindset.context: Finish the opening exchange in the stronger phase or safely back at centre.

instructions: Recall the familiar route-A opening and its intended phase.
Name the one reaction that triggers the rehearsed route-B transition.
Close on the no-structure danger cue and the trusted centre reset.
progress: Rehearse only the two known routes during fight week.

name: First Transition Cue (MMA)
why: Lock in the first familiar signal for changing phase.

mindset.intent: Switch once, decisively, when the trained reaction appears.
mindset.focus: The single posture or distance cue repeatedly used in camp.
mindset.reset: Danger cue: the reaction is incomplete; stay in the current phase and restore stance.
mindset.anchor: No cue, no switch.
mindset.context: Finish stable in the new phase with the next offence available.

instructions: Name the one reaction retained as the transition signal.
Visualise the familiar phase switch and its finishing position.
Rehearse one absent-cue example followed by the known stance reset.
progress: Carry this single transition rule into the final review.

name: Ring Route Scan (Kickboxing)
why: Learn which ring exit the opponent chooses first when pressure removes open space.

mindset.intent: Cut off the preferred lane without following directly behind their movement.
mindset.focus: First circle, pivot, stance switch or straight retreat as the boundary approaches.
mindset.reset: If the route changes, hold centre in stance and begin the cut again.
mindset.anchor: Take the lane before taking the exchange.
mindset.context: Finish facing the opponent with centre owned and both kick and punch defence available.
